::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Give every rule a `log:` and a `benchmark:`, and read a benchmark file.
- Use `threads:` and `params:`, and explain why a setting belongs in `params`.
- Mark outputs `temp()` or `protected()` and predict what that does to reruns.
- Give a rule its own conda environment, and avoid the two traps that come
  with it.
- Write shell commands with literal braces, and let a known tool failure pass
  on purpose.

Time: 50 min
:::

## One rule, all the directives

This is `align` at stopping point B. Compare it with the module 2 version:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" rule="align" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The command is the same `bowtie2 | samtools sort` pipe. Everything around it
is new: where its messages go (`log`), how long it took (`benchmark`), how
many cores it may use (`threads`), the settings it reads (`params`), what may
be deleted later (`temp`) and which software it runs in (`conda`). The rest of
this module takes them one at a time.
:::

## `log:`

```python
    log:
        LOGS + "/align/{sample}.log",
    shell:
        "bowtie2 ... 2> {log} | samtools sort ... 2>> {log}"
```

`log:` declares a file per job, with the same wildcards as the output. It
does not capture anything by itself: you redirect into `{log}` in the command.
Here bowtie2's alignment summary goes in with `2>`, and samtools appends with
`2>>`, so one file holds both.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two things make logs different from outputs. A failed job's outputs are
deleted, but its log is kept, which is exactly when you need it. And a log
never triggers a rerun. A rule whose tool prints to stdout and stderr in one
command uses `> {log} 2>&1` (see `bowtie2_index` and `call_peaks`). A rule
with several commands empties the log once (`: > {log}`) and then appends
(see `consensus_peaks`).
:::

## `benchmark:`

```python
    benchmark:
        BENCH + "/align/{sample}.tsv",
```

Snakemake measures the job while it runs and writes one line of numbers:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-benchmark | stopping-points/stopB | snakemake --cores 4 output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam > /dev/null 2>&1; cat output/benchmarks/bowtie2_index/bowtie2_index.tsv -->

```bash
cat output/benchmarks/bowtie2_index/bowtie2_index.tsv
```

{{< generated name="stopB-benchmark" command="false" >}}

`s` is wall-clock seconds, `max_rss` the peak memory in MB, `cpu_time` the CPU
seconds used by the job's processes. On a cluster these numbers are how you
choose memory and time requests (module 5). Exercise 4.3 reads them.

## `threads:`

```python
    threads: 4
    shell:
        "bowtie2 -p {threads} ..."
```

`threads:` is what the rule may use, and `{threads}` passes it to the tool.
Snakemake fits jobs into `--cores`: with `--cores 4`, it runs one 4-thread
`align` at a time, or two 2-thread `filter` jobs side by side. Ask for
`--cores 2` and `align` is given 2 threads ("Rules claiming more threads will
be scaled down").

::: {.notes}
The tool does not know about `threads:` unless the command passes it. A rule
that says `threads: 8` and runs `bowtie2` without `-p` blocks 8 cores and
uses 1.
:::

## `params:`: settings the rule depends on

In module 3 the MAPQ cutoff became a global variable read from the config.
That has a hole. Change `MIN_MAPQ` from 30 to 20 in stopping point A, where
everything has run, and ask again:

```text
Building DAG of jobs...
Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).
```

Snakemake does not see the change: the rule's code (`-q {MIN_MAPQ}`) is the
same text, and no file changed. As a `param`, the value is recorded with each
output:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" lines="203-205" >}}

## A param change reruns what used it

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-params-rerun | stopping-points/stopB | snakemake --cores 4 output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak > /dev/null 2>&1 && snakemake -n output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak --config minMapq=20 2>&1 | grep -E '^rule |reason:' -->

```bash
snakemake -n output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak --config minMapq=20
```

{{< generated name="stopB-params-rerun" command="false" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Both `filter` jobs (the sample and its control) rerun because their params
changed, and the peak call reruns because its inputs will be new. Why does
`align` rerun too? Its output is `temp()`, so it was deleted after `filter`
used it, and `filter` needs it again. That is the price of `temp()`.

Params can also be functions of `wildcards`, `input` or `output`, like the
`-c` flag in `call_peaks` (module 3) or `params.outdir` there.
:::

## Turning the extra triggers off

Sometimes you do not want that. You fixed a typo in a comment, or switched
from the course env to conda, and the results cannot have changed.
`--rerun-triggers mtime` goes back to timestamps only:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-params-mtime | stopping-points/stopB | snakemake --cores 4 output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak > /dev/null 2>&1 && snakemake -n output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak --config minMapq=20 --rerun-triggers mtime 2>&1 | grep -v 'strict channel priorities' -->

```bash
snakemake -n output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak --config minMapq=20 --rerun-triggers mtime
```

{{< generated name="stopB-params-mtime" command="false" >}}

The default in Snakemake 8 is all five triggers: `mtime`, `params`, `input`,
`software-env` and `code`. Use `mtime` alone on purpose, for one run, and know
that the BAMs you keep were made with MAPQ 30.

## `temp()` and `protected()`

```python
    output:
        bam = temp(OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_aligned.bam"),
```

`temp()` deletes a file as soon as every job that needs it has finished. The
sorted-but-unfiltered BAMs are the biggest files in RegPipe and nobody looks
at them; a full run prints `Removing temporary output ...` ten times.

`protected()` does the opposite. It makes outputs read-only after the job, so
nothing overwrites them by accident:

```python
    output:
        protected(multiext(OUT + "/reference/bowtie2_index/genome",
                           ".1.bt2", ".2.bt2", ".3.bt2", ".4.bt2", ".rev.1.bt2", ".rev.2.bt2")),
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
After the job you see `Write-protecting output file ...` for each file. If a
later run would rebuild them, Snakemake stops with an error instead of
overwriting.<!-- VERIFY-DATA --> To rebuild on
purpose, delete the files yourself. Use it for things that are slow to make
and that many jobs depend on: an index, a big reference download. Rebuilding
the index in stopping point B makes 40 jobs out of date (every `align`,
everything after it, and `rule all`), so it is a good candidate. Stopping point B leaves
it unprotected so you can experiment.
:::

## `conda:`

```python
    conda: "envs/regpipe_align.yml"
```

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="envs/regpipe_align.yml" >}}

```bash
snakemake --cores 4 --sdm conda      # --use-conda is the older spelling, same effect
```

The first run builds each environment once (about a minute for the three in
stopping point B) and keeps it in `.snakemake/conda/`. Each job then runs
with its rule's environment activated, so you no longer depend on what
happens to be installed in your shell.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The pins (`samtools=1.24`) are the point. A result made with this rule says
which samtools made it, and next year's run gets the same version. Snakemake
also warns at every start that conda is "not configured to use strict channel
priorities"; run `conda config --set channel_priority strict` once to silence
it and get more predictable solves.
:::

## Two conda traps

The first: Snakemake 8.27.1 runs `conda info` for any rule that has a
`conda:` directive, even when you run without `--sdm conda`. If `conda` is not
on your `PATH`, those jobs fail with `Error running conda info`. Keep conda
available in the shell you launch from.

The second: switching how software is provided counts as a change. When we
first ran stopping point B with tools from the course env and then again with
`--sdm conda`, every job was planned again with the reason
`Software environment definition has changed`. A dry run does not warn you,
because the environments do not exist yet when it runs. Add
`--rerun-triggers mtime` for that first conda run if the outputs are good.

::: {.notes}
The second trap also deleted four FastQC outputs as "incomplete" when that
rerun was interrupted. Interrupt a run and Snakemake cleans up what was in
flight; that is usually what you want, but not when the files were fine.
:::

## Which Python?

Inside a job, the rule's conda environment comes first on `PATH`, but not
always. On the cluster, the lab launchers keep a virtual environment with
Snakemake in it, and its `bin/` can end up ahead. A bare `python` then finds
the wrong interpreter and fails with `No module named ...`. MicroCPipe names
the interpreter of the rule's own environment:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="180-195" >}}

`$CONDA_PREFIX` is set by conda inside the job. Snakemake leaves `$NAME` alone
(it only fills `{...}`), so bash expands it when the job runs.

## Literal braces in a shell command

Snakemake fills in everything in `{...}`. awk uses braces too:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-awk-braces | stopping-points/stopB | cat >> Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule count_peaks:
    input:
        peaks = OUT + "/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak",
    output:
        OUT + "/peaks/{sample}_peak_count.txt",
    shell:
        "awk '{n++} END {print FILENAME, n}' {input.peaks} > {output}"
EOF
snakemake -n -p output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peak_count.txt 2>&1 | sed -n '/^RuleException/,$p' || true -->

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule count_peaks:
    input:
        peaks = OUT + "/peaks/{sample}_peaks.narrowPeak",
    output:
        OUT + "/peaks/{sample}_peak_count.txt",
    shell:
        "awk '{n++} END {print FILENAME, n}' {input.peaks} > {output}"
```

{{< generated name="stopB-awk-braces" command="false" >}}

The message gives the fix: double the braces that are not Snakemake's,
`awk '{{n++}} END {{print FILENAME, n}}'`. With that, the job writes
`output/peaks/HCT116_CTCF_1_peaks.narrowPeak 24`: 24 CTCF peaks for
replicate 1.

## Failing on purpose, gracefully

Strict mode makes any failing command fail the job. Sometimes a tool fails
for a reason that says something about the data, not the pipeline. MicroCPipe
runs preseq, which refuses to extrapolate a library that is too shallow:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" rule="library_complexity" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`preseq ... || {{ ... }}` runs the block only if preseq fails. The braces are
bash's command grouping, doubled because they are literal. The fallback
warns on stderr and writes a header-only table, so the output exists and the
report downstream shows "no data" for that library. The comment above says
which error and why it is safe to continue. Write that comment every time
you swallow an error.
:::

## Exercise 4.1: Fix the rule

This rule should write each sample's filtered read count, and send
everything the tools print to its log. It fails. Find both problems.

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule count_reads:
    input:
        bam = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam",
    output:
        OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_read_count.txt",
    log:
        LOGS + "/count_reads/{sample}.log",
    threads: 2
    shell:
        """
        samtools view -c -@ {threads} {input.bam} | awk '{print "{wildcards.sample}", $1}' > {output} 2> {log}
        """
```

[Answer](../answers/04-rules-that-behave-answers.qmd#ex-4.1)
:::

## Stopping point B

::: {.callout-important .stopping-point}
## Stopping point B: end of day 1

`stopping-points/stopB/` is RegPipe at the end of day 1: the samplesheet and
config, input functions for the controls, peaks, consensus peaks and bigWigs,
and every rule with a log, a benchmark, threads, params and a conda
environment. A dry run plans 51 jobs.

Day 2 starts from here. If your own copy does not run, use this one:

```bash
cp -r stopping-points/stopB work/regpipe-B
cd work/regpipe-B
snakemake -n
snakemake --cores 4 --sdm conda
```
:::

## Key points

- `log:` keeps each job's messages, even when it fails; you redirect into it.
  `benchmark:` records time and memory per job.
- `threads:` is what a job may use; pass it to the tool with `{threads}`.
- Put settings in `params:`. Then a changed setting reruns the jobs that used
  it, and only those.
- `temp()` saves disk and costs a rerun later; `protected()` guards outputs
  that are slow to rebuild.
- `conda:` pins each rule's software. Keep conda on `PATH`, and expect one
  full rerun the first time you switch to it (or use `--rerun-triggers mtime`).
- Double the braces that belong to awk or bash: `{{` and `}}`.

Day 2 starts with [Module 5, Running on a cluster](05-cluster.qmd).
